quiz.q: In ΔABC, DE ∥ BC with AD = 6 cm, DB = 9 cm and AE = 8 cm. What is EC?
quiz.explain: AD/DB = AE/EC gives 6/9 = 8/EC, so EC = 8 × 9 ÷ 6 = 12 cm.
quiz.mistake: Flips the ratio and gets 8 × 6 ÷ 9 ≈ 5.33

quiz.q: In ΔABC, D is on AB and E is on AC with AD = 3, DB = 5, AE = 4.5 and EC = 7.5. Is DE ∥ BC?
options: No, because the sides are not equal
Yes, by the converse of BPT
quiz.explain: AD/DB = 3/5 = 0.6 and AE/EC = 4.5/7.5 = 0.6. The ratios are equal, so DE ∥ BC by the converse of BPT.
quiz.mistake: Expects the pieces to be equal rather than in the same ratio

quiz.q: In ΔABC, DE ∥ BC and AD/DB = 2/3. If AC = 20 cm, what is AE?
quiz.explain: AE/EC = 2/3, so AE is 2 parts out of 5 parts of AC: AE = 2/5 × 20 = 8 cm.
quiz.mistake: Uses 2/3 of AC instead of 2/5

quiz.q: In ΔABC, DE ∥ BC with AD = x, DB = x − 3, AE = x + 3 and EC = x − 2. Find x.
quiz.mistake: Makes a sign error when expanding (x + 3)(x − 3)

quiz.q: In ΔPQR, ST ∥ QR with S on PQ and T on PR. If PS/SQ = 3/4, what is PT/PR?
quiz.explain: PT/TR = 3/4, so PT is 3 parts of the 7 parts of PR: PT/PR = 3/7.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the part-to-part ratio with the part-to-whole ratio

quiz.q: D and E are the midpoints of AB and AC in ΔABC, and BC = 14 cm. What is DE?
quiz.explain: The segment joining the midpoints of two sides is parallel to the third side and half of it: 14 ÷ 2 = 7 cm.
quiz.mistake: Thinks DE equals BC because they are parallel

quiz.q: By what other name is the Basic Proportionality Theorem known?
quiz.explain: It is named after the Greek mathematician Thales.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the names of famous theorems

quiz.q: ABCD is a trapezium with AB ∥ DC, and its diagonals meet at O. Which ratio equals AO/OC?
quiz.explain: Draw a line through O parallel to AB and DC and apply BPT in two triangles. This shows the diagonals cut each other in the same ratio: AO/OC = BO/OD.
quiz.mistake: Writes the second ratio upside down

teach.ask: Gappu draws a line across a triangle: 'When does this line cut the sides in the same ratio?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Parallel to one side means the other two sides are cut in the same ratio. Thales says hi!
teach.nudge: What must be true about the line, and what happens to the two sides it cuts?

learn.hook: You don't need to check all six parts — just the right three clues prove two triangles are similar!
points: AAA (or AA) criterion: if two angles of one triangle equal two angles of another, the triangles are similar (the third angles are then equal too).
SSS criterion: if all three pairs of corresponding sides are in the same ratio, the triangles are similar.
SAS criterion: if one angle is equal and the sides including that angle are in the same ratio, the triangles are similar.
For triangles, equal angles guarantee proportional sides and proportional sides guarantee equal angles.
SSA is NOT a similarity criterion. Always write the vertices in the matching order.

example.q: A girl 1.5 m tall casts a 2 m shadow. At the same time a pole casts a 12 m shadow. How tall is the pole?
steps: The sun's rays make the same angle with the ground, and both stand at 90°, so the triangles are similar (AA)

learn.reallife: Surveyors find the height of a temple tower or a tall tree using a stick and shadows — no climbing needed!

games.title: Name the criterion
pairs: All three sides in the same ratio
One equal angle with the sides around it in the same ratio
A line parallel to one side of a triangle

games.title: Similar or not?
items: If two angles of one triangle equal two angles of another, the triangles are similar.
The third angles must also match, since each triangle's angles add to 180°.
SSA is a similarity criterion.
Two sides and a non-included angle do not fix the shape.
Triangles with sides 3, 4, 5 and 6, 8, 10 are similar.
Each ratio is 2, so they are similar by SSS.
Triangles with sides 2, 3, 4 and 4, 6, 9 are similar.
If ΔABC ~ ΔDEF, then AB/DE = BC/EF = CA/FD.
Corresponding sides follow the order of the letters.
Two triangles with one pair of equal angles are always similar.
One equal angle is not enough; you need two.

quiz.q: Two triangles have sides 4, 6, 8 cm and 6, 9, 12 cm. Are they similar, and by which criterion?
quiz.explain: 6/4 = 9/6 = 12/8 = 1.5. All three sides are in the same ratio, so the triangles are similar by SSS.
quiz.mistake: Thinks sides must be equal, not just proportional

quiz.q: Meena, 1.5 m tall, casts a 2.5 m shadow. At the same time a tower casts a 40 m shadow. How tall is the tower?
quiz.explain: The triangles are similar (AA), so height/shadow is equal: 1.5/2.5 = h/40, giving h = 24 m.
quiz.mistake: Uses shadow/height on one side and height/shadow on the other

quiz.q: In ΔABC and ΔPQR, ∠A = ∠P = 40° and AB/PQ = AC/PR = 2/3. By which criterion are they similar?
quiz.explain: An equal angle (∠A = ∠P) with the sides including it in the same ratio is the SAS criterion.
quiz.mistake: Calls it SSS without having the third pair of sides

quiz.q: In ΔABC, ∠A = 65° and ∠B = 45°. In ΔDEF, ∠D = 65° and ∠F = 70°. Are the two triangles similar, and with which vertex order?
options: Only if the sides are equal
quiz.mistake: Writes the vertices in the wrong matching order

quiz.q: ΔABC ~ ΔPQR, with AB = 3 cm, BC = 4 cm, CA = 5 cm and PQ = 6 cm. What is the perimeter of ΔPQR?
quiz.explain: The scale factor is 6/3 = 2, so the perimeter is 2 × (3 + 4 + 5) = 24 cm.
quiz.mistake: Gives the perimeter of ΔABC

quiz.q: In ΔABC, DE ∥ BC with D on AB and E on AC. AD = 2 cm, AB = 6 cm and DE = 3 cm. What is BC?
quiz.explain: ΔADE ~ ΔABC by AA (corresponding angles are equal). So DE/BC = AD/AB = 2/6, giving BC = 3 × 6 ÷ 2 = 9 cm.
quiz.mistake: Uses AD/DB = 2/4 instead of AD/AB

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a criterion for similarity of triangles?
quiz.explain: Two sides and an angle that is not between them do not fix the shape of a triangle.
quiz.mistake: Assumes any three parts are enough

quiz.q: In right ΔABC with ∠B = 90°, BD is drawn perpendicular to AC. Which triangle is ΔADB similar to?
quiz.explain: In ΔADB and ΔABC, ∠A is common and ∠ADB = ∠ABC = 90°. By AA, A ↔ A, D ↔ B, B ↔ C, so ΔADB ~ ΔABC.
quiz.mistake: Gets the order of the matching vertices wrong

teach.ask: Gappu has two triangles: 'Do I have to measure everything to know they are similar?'
teach.praise: Tweet tweet! AA, SSS or SAS — any one of these clues is enough. Detective Gappu is ready!
teach.nudge: What are the three shortcuts, and do sides need to be equal or just in the same ratio?

learn.hook: Once two triangles are similar, a whole treasure of equal ratios, products and angles opens up!
points: In the current book, the AA, SSS and SAS criteria are stated and used without proof — your job is to pick the right criterion and match the vertices correctly.
From similar triangles, write equal ratios and cross-multiply: if ΔPAC ~ ΔPDB then PA/PD = PC/PB, so PA × PB = PC × PD.
In similar triangles, corresponding medians and altitudes are in the same ratio as corresponding sides.
When two lines cross at O and AC ∥ BD, ΔOAC ~ ΔOBD (vertically opposite angles and alternate angles are equal).
In a right triangle ABC (∠C = 90°) with CD ⊥ AB: ΔACD ~ ΔABC, so AC² = AB × AD.

example.q: ΔABC ~ ΔPQR with AB = 6 cm and PQ = 9 cm. The median AD of ΔABC is 4 cm. Find the median PM of ΔPQR.
steps: Corresponding medians are in the ratio of the sides

learn.reallife: Architects use these ratios to scale every part of a building plan — not just the outer walls but every beam and diagonal.

games.title: Match the similarity to the result
pairs: ΔABC ~ ΔPQR with medians AD, PM

games.title: True or false?
items: In the current book, the SSS and SAS criteria are used without proof.
They are stated as results to apply.
Corresponding altitudes of similar triangles are in the ratio of their sides.
This follows from AA similarity of the smaller right triangles.
If two lines cross at O and AC ∥ BD, then ΔOAC ~ ΔOBD.
Vertically opposite angles at O and alternate angles give AA.
Ratios from similar triangles can be written in any vertex order.
The order must follow the correspondence of vertices.
If PA/PD = PC/PB, then PA × PD = PC × PB.
Cross-multiplying gives PA × PB = PC × PD.

quiz.q: ΔABC ~ ΔPQR with AB = 6 cm and PQ = 9 cm. The median AD is 4 cm. What is the corresponding median PM?
quiz.explain: Medians are in the ratio of the sides: PM = 4 × 9/6 = 6 cm.
quiz.mistake: Turns the ratio upside down

quiz.q: ΔABC ~ ΔDEF with BC = 8 cm and EF = 12 cm. The altitude from A is 6 cm. What is the altitude from D?
quiz.explain: Altitudes are in the ratio of the sides: 6 × 12/8 = 9 cm.
quiz.mistake: Adds the difference of sides instead of using the ratio

quiz.q: In trapezium ABCD with AB ∥ DC, the diagonals meet at O. OA = 6 cm, OC = 4 cm and OB = 9 cm. What is OD?
quiz.explain: ΔOAB ~ ΔOCD (AA), so OA/OC = OB/OD. 6/4 = 9/OD gives OD = 6 cm.
quiz.mistake: Matches OB with OC instead of OD

quiz.q: Lines AB and CD cross at O with AC ∥ BD. OA = 4 cm, OB = 6 cm and AC = 5 cm. What is BD?
quiz.explain: ΔOAC ~ ΔOBD (vertically opposite and alternate angles). So BD/AC = OB/OA → BD = 5 × 6/4 = 7.5 cm.
quiz.mistake: Uses the ratio upside down

quiz.q: From ΔPAC ~ ΔPDB, we get PA/PD = PC/PB. Which result follows?
quiz.explain: Cross-multiplying PA/PD = PC/PB gives PA × PB = PC × PD.
quiz.mistake: Cross-multiplies the wrong pairs

quiz.q: You are told the SAS similarity criterion without proof. What must you still check before using it?
options: That one angle is equal and the sides including it are in the same ratio
Nothing — any two triangles are similar
quiz.explain: SAS needs one pair of equal angles with the two sides making that angle in the same ratio.
quiz.mistake: Uses SAS with an angle that is not between the two sides

quiz.q: ΔODC ~ ΔOBA, where B, O, D lie on one straight line. If ∠BOC = 130°, what is ∠DOC?
quiz.explain: ∠BOC and ∠DOC form a linear pair on line BD, so ∠DOC = 180° − 130° = 50°.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the two angles are equal instead of adding to 180°

quiz.q: In the same figure (ΔODC ~ ΔOBA, ∠DOC = 50°), ∠CDO = 65°. What is ∠OAB?
quiz.mistake: Matches the vertices in the wrong order

quiz.q: In right ΔABC with ∠C = 90°, CD ⊥ AB. If AB = 9 cm and AD = 4 cm, what is AC?
quiz.explain: ΔACD ~ ΔABC gives AC/AB = AD/AC, so AC² = AB × AD = 36 and AC = 6 cm.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to take the square root

teach.ask: Gappu knows ΔPAC ~ ΔPDB but doesn't know what to do next. Show him how to get a useful result.
teach.praise: Tweet! Write the matching ratios in the right order, cross-multiply — and out pops PA × PB = PC × PD!
teach.nudge: Which sides go together in the ratios?

learn.hook: Walk away from a street lamp at night and your shadow stretches longer and longer. Similar triangles tell you exactly how long!
points: Lamp-post problems: the lamp-post and the person are both vertical, and the light ray makes the same angle with the ground. So the two triangles are similar (AA).
If the lamp is H high, the person h high, the person stands d from the post and the shadow is s long, then h/H = s/(s + d).
The farther the person walks, the longer the shadow.
Recap: similar figures; BPT and its converse; AA (AAA), SSS and SAS criteria for similar triangles.

example.q: A street lamp is 4.5 m high. A boy 1.5 m tall stands 6 m from its foot. How long is his shadow?
steps: Let the shadow be s m. Big triangle: height 4.5, base s + 6. Small triangle: height 1.5, base s

learn.reallife: Photographers and stage-lighting crews use this idea to predict how long a shadow will fall on the floor.

games.title: Solving a lamp-post problem
items: Draw the lamp-post, the person and the light ray
Spot two similar right triangles (AA)
Let the shadow be s and write h/H = s/(s + d)
Cross-multiply and solve for s
Check the answer is sensible (positive, not too long)

games.title: Recap: match the result
pairs: Line ∥ one side cuts the other two in the same ratio
Line cutting two sides in the same ratio is ∥ third side
One equal angle and including sides proportional

quiz.q: A street lamp is 4.5 m high. A boy 1.5 m tall stands 6 m from its foot. How long is his shadow?
quiz.mistake: Uses s/6 instead of s/(s + 6)

quiz.q: A lamp is 5 m high. Pooja, 1.25 m tall, walks away from it at 1 m/s. How long is her shadow after 6 seconds?
quiz.explain: After 6 s she is 6 m away. 1.25/5 = s/(s + 6) → 4s = s + 6 → s = 2 m.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to add the distance walked to the shadow for the big triangle

quiz.q: As a girl walks away from a lamp-post, what happens to the length of her shadow?
quiz.explain: s = hd/(H − h) grows as the distance d grows, so the shadow gets longer.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the shadow behaves like a sunlight shadow, which does not depend on distance

quiz.q: At the same moment, a 2 m stick casts a 1.6 m shadow and a tower casts a 24 m shadow. How tall is the tower?
quiz.explain: Height/shadow is the same: h/24 = 2/1.6, so h = 24 × 2/1.6 = 30 m.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by 1.6/2 instead of 2/1.6

quiz.q: Recap: in ΔABC, DE ∥ BC with AD/DB = 3/5 and AE = 6 cm. What is EC?
quiz.explain: By BPT, AE/EC = AD/DB = 3/5, so EC = 6 × 5/3 = 10 cm.
quiz.mistake: Turns the ratio the wrong way

quiz.q: Recap: two triangles have two pairs of equal angles. Which criterion says they are similar?
quiz.explain: Two equal angles force the third to be equal too, so AA (or AAA) applies.
quiz.mistake: Confuses similarity criteria with congruence criteria like RHS

quiz.q: Recap: are triangles with sides 5, 12, 13 cm and 10, 24, 26 cm similar?
options: Yes, by SSS, since every ratio is 1/2
No, only equilateral triangles can be similar
quiz.explain: 5/10 = 12/24 = 13/26 = 1/2, so the sides are proportional and SSS applies.
quiz.mistake: Thinks similar triangles must have equal sides

quiz.q: Recap: in ΔPQR, points S on PQ and T on PR satisfy PS/SQ = PT/TR. What can you conclude?
quiz.explain: By the converse of BPT, a line dividing two sides in the same ratio is parallel to the third side.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up BPT with its converse or with congruence

teach.ask: Gappu stands under a street lamp at night and wonders how long his shadow is. Explain how similar triangles help.
teach.praise: Chirp! The lamp-post and I make similar triangles, so h/H = s/(s + d). I can find my shadow!

topics.title: Coordinates refresher and where the distance formula comes from

learn.hook: Every spot on a map has an address of two numbers. Pythagoras turns those addresses into distances!
points: The x-axis and y-axis meet at the origin O(0, 0) and divide the plane into four quadrants: I (+, +), II (−, +), III (−, −), IV (+, −).
In (x, y), x is the abscissa (distance from the y-axis) and y is the ordinate (distance from the x-axis).
Every point on the x-axis is (x, 0) and every point on the y-axis is (0, y).
Coordinate geometry is used in maps, GPS, physics and engineering to turn shapes into numbers.
Distance formula idea: from P(x₁, y₁) to Q(x₂, y₂), draw a right triangle with horizontal side |x₂ − x₁| and vertical side |y₂ − y₁|. Pythagoras gives PQ² = (x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)².

example.q: Use Pythagoras to find the distance between P(1, 2) and Q(4, 6).
steps: Draw a horizontal line from P and a vertical line from Q; they meet at R(4, 2)

learn.reallife: Delivery apps place your home and the restaurant as coordinates and use exactly this formula to estimate the straight-line distance.

games.title: Match the point to its quadrant

quiz.q: In which quadrant does the point (−3, 5) lie?
quiz.explain: x is negative and y is positive, which is Quadrant II.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the signs of the quadrants

quiz.q: What is the abscissa of the point (7, −2)?
quiz.explain: The abscissa is the x-coordinate, so it is 7.
quiz.mistake: Confuses abscissa with ordinate

quiz.q: Where does the point (0, −4) lie?
quiz.explain: Its x-coordinate is 0, so it is on the y-axis, 4 units below the origin.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a 0 in the first place means the x-axis

quiz.q: Which form does every point on the x-axis have?
quiz.explain: On the x-axis the height above it is zero, so y = 0.
quiz.mistake: Swaps the forms for the two axes

quiz.q: What is the distance between (3, 2) and (3, 9)?
quiz.explain: Both points have x = 3, so they are on one vertical line. Distance = 9 − 2 = 7.
steps: Same x, so the distance is the difference of y
quiz.mistake: Adds the y-values instead of subtracting

quiz.q: To find PQ for P(x₁, y₁) and Q(x₂, y₂), we draw a right triangle with PQ as its hypotenuse. Pythagoras gives PQ² = ?
quiz.explain: The two shorter sides are the horizontal gap (x₂ − x₁) and the vertical gap (y₂ − y₁). Square and add them.
quiz.mistake: Adds coordinates instead of subtracting, or forgets to square

quiz.q: For P(1, 2) and Q(4, 6), what is the length of the horizontal side of the right triangle with hypotenuse PQ?
quiz.explain: The horizontal side goes from x = 1 to x = 4, so it is 4 − 1 = 3. (The vertical side is 6 − 2 = 4 and PQ = 5.)
quiz.mistake: Uses the change in y instead of the change in x

quiz.q: Which of these is a real use of coordinate geometry?

quiz.explain: GPS gives each place coordinates and uses them to find positions and distances.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect coordinates with maps and positions

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Where does the distance formula come from? It looks like magic!' Explain it to him.
teach.praise: Chirp! The horizontal gap and vertical gap make a right triangle — Pythagoras does the rest!
teach.nudge: What are the two shorter sides of that right triangle?

learn.hook: Pythagoras goes to the graph paper: find the distance between any two points without a ruler!
points: The distance between P(x₁, y₁) and Q(x₂, y₂) is PQ = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²].
It comes from Pythagoras theorem: the horizontal gap and the vertical gap are the two shorter sides of a right triangle.
The distance of P(x, y) from the origin O(0, 0) is √(x² + y²).
The order of the points does not matter, because the differences are squared.
If the points are on the same horizontal or vertical line, the distance is just the difference of the changing coordinate.

example.q: Find the distance between A(−2, 3) and B(4, −5).

learn.reallife: Map apps work out straight-line distances between places using coordinates, just like this formula.

games.title: Match the points to their distance

quiz.q: What is the distance between (2, 3) and (10, 9)?
quiz.mistake: Adds the gaps (8 + 6 = 14) instead of using squares

quiz.q: How far is the point (−5, 12) from the origin?
quiz.mistake: Treats (−5)² as −25

quiz.q: What is the distance between (a, 0) and (0, a), where a > 0?
quiz.mistake: Adds the two gaps and gets 2a

quiz.q: The points (1, k) and (4, 5) are 5 units apart. What can k be?
quiz.explain: 3² + (5 − k)² = 25 gives (5 − k)² = 16, so 5 − k = ±4 and k = 1 or 9.
quiz.mistake: Takes only the positive square root

quiz.q: On a town map, Riya's house is at (2, 1) and her school at (8, 9), where 1 unit = 100 m. How far apart are they in a straight line?
quiz.explain: Distance = √(6² + 8²) = 10 units, and 10 × 100 m = 1000 m.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to use the map scale, or adds 6 + 8

quiz.q: What is the distance between (−6, 2) and (−2, −1)?
quiz.explain: Δx = −2 − (−6) = 4 and Δy = −1 − 2 = −3, so the distance is √(16 + 9) = 5.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to take the square root (25) or mishandles the negative signs

quiz.q: What is the distance of the point (x, y) from the origin?
quiz.explain: Use the distance formula with (0, 0): √[(x − 0)² + (y − 0)²] = √(x² + y²).
quiz.mistake: Forgets the square root, or adds the coordinates

quiz.q: Which point is nearest to the origin?
quiz.mistake: Ignores negative coordinates or just adds the coordinates

teach.ask: Gappu sits at (1, 2) and his friend at (4, 6): 'How far apart are we on this graph?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Subtract, square, add and take the square root. We are 5 units apart!

topics.title: Using distances: shapes and collinear points

learn.hook: With just the distance formula you can prove points are in a straight line, or spot a hidden square!
points: Points A, B, C are collinear (on one line) if the two shorter distances add up to the longest, e.g. AB + BC = AC.
Isosceles triangle: two sides equal. Equilateral: all three sides equal.
Right triangle: the square of the longest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two (converse of Pythagoras).
Quadrilaterals: four equal sides and equal diagonals → square; four equal sides only → rhombus; opposite sides equal and equal diagonals → rectangle.
To find a point equidistant from A and B, set PA² = PB² (squares avoid messy roots).

example.q: Show that A(1, 1), B(4, 5) and C(7, 9) are collinear.
steps: AB + BC = 5 + 5 = 10 = AC, so the points lie on one line
example.answer: A, B and C are collinear

learn.reallife: Planners check whether three bus stops lie on one straight road, or whether a plot of land is a perfect square, using coordinates.

games.title: Shape spotter
items: If AB + BC = AC, then A, B and C are collinear.
B lies on the segment AC, so all three are on one line.
A quadrilateral with four equal sides is always a square.
It could be a rhombus with no right angle; the diagonals must also be equal for a square.
The points (0, 0), (3, 0) and (0, 4) form a right triangle.
The sides are 3, 4 and 5, and 3² + 4² = 5².
The points (0, 0), (2, 0) and (1, √3) form an equilateral triangle.
Each side is 2: for example √(1² + (√3)²) = √4 = 2.
The points (1, 2), (2, 3) and (4, 6) are collinear.
√2 + √13 ≈ 5.02, which is not equal to the longest distance 5.
The point (3, 3) is equidistant from (0, 0) and (6, 0).
Both distances are √18.

games.title: Find the point on the x-axis equidistant from A(3, 4) and B(−1, 2)

Set PA² = PB²

quiz.q: Are the points A(1, 5), B(2, 3) and C(−2, 11) collinear?
options: No, because no two distances are equal
Yes, because all distances are equal
No, because they form a right triangle
quiz.explain: AB = √5, AC = √45 = 3√5 and BC = √80 = 4√5. Since √5 + 3√5 = 4√5, AB + AC = BC, so the points are collinear.

quiz.q: What kind of triangle has vertices A(0, 0), B(4, 0) and C(4, 3)?
quiz.explain: AB = 4, BC = 3 and AC = 5. Since 3² + 4² = 5², the angle at B is 90°.
quiz.mistake: Does not test the Pythagoras condition

quiz.q: Which point on the y-axis is equidistant from (2, 3) and (−4, 1)?
quiz.explain: Let P = (0, y). 4 + (y − 3)² = 16 + (y − 1)² gives −6y + 13 = −2y + 17, so y = −1. Both distances are √20.
quiz.mistake: Takes a point on the x-axis instead of the y-axis

quiz.q: What figure do the points (1, 1), (4, 1), (4, 4) and (1, 4) form?
options: A rhombus that is not a square
A rectangle that is not a square
quiz.explain: All four sides are 3 and both diagonals are √18 = 3√2. Equal sides with equal diagonals make a square.
quiz.mistake: Checks the sides but not the diagonals

quiz.q: P(x, 3) is equidistant from A(1, 1) and B(5, 1). What is x?
quiz.mistake: Makes an error expanding the squares

quiz.q: A circle has centre (2, −1) and passes through (5, 3). What is its radius?
quiz.explain: The radius is the distance from the centre to the point: √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to take the square root, or adds the gaps

quiz.q: What kind of triangle has vertices (0, 0), (6, 0) and (3, 4)?
quiz.explain: The sides are 6, √(9 + 16) = 5 and √(9 + 16) = 5. Two equal sides make it isosceles; 5² + 5² ≠ 6², so it is not right-angled.
quiz.mistake: Assumes a triangle with whole-number sides is right-angled

quiz.q: Three laddoo stalls at a mela are at (3, 1), (6, 4) and (8, 6). Are they in a straight line?
options: No, because the first two gaps are unequal
Yes, because they are in the same row
quiz.explain: AB = √18 = 3√2, BC = √8 = 2√2 and AC = √50 = 5√2. Since 3√2 + 2√2 = 5√2, the stalls are collinear.
quiz.mistake: Thinks collinear points must be equally spaced

teach.ask: Gappu has three points: 'How can I prove they lie on one straight line?'
teach.praise: Tweet! If the two shorter distances add up to the longest one, they're on one line!

topics.title: Equidistant points and checking seating patterns

learn.hook: Are four friends sitting in a perfect square in class? Don't trust your eyes — trust the distance formula!
points: A point P(x, y) is equidistant from A and B when PA = PB. Square both sides (PA² = PB²) and simplify to get a relation between x and y.
The x² and y² terms cancel, so the relation is a straight line — it is the perpendicular bisector of AB.
To test a square: all four sides equal AND both diagonals equal. Equal sides only → rhombus. Opposite sides equal and equal diagonals → rectangle.
Seating or garden layouts given as coordinates can be checked this way.

example.q: Find a relation between x and y if P(x, y) is equidistant from A(2, 1) and B(4, 5).

learn.reallife: Event planners lay out chairs, stalls and rangoli squares on a grid and check the distances before the big day.

Check that all four sides are equal
Find the two diagonals

games.title: Square, rhombus or rectangle?
items: Four equal sides are enough to prove a square.
A rhombus also has four equal sides; the diagonals must be equal too.
A quadrilateral with four equal sides and equal diagonals is a square.
That is the test for a square.
Points equidistant from A and B lie on a straight line.
The relation from PA² = PB² is linear: the perpendicular bisector of AB.
(5, 2) is equidistant from (2, 1) and (4, 5).
Both distances are √10.
Equal diagonals and four equal sides can also describe a rectangle that is not a square.
A rectangle that is not a square does not have four equal sides.

quiz.q: P(x, y) is equidistant from A(2, 1) and B(4, 5). Which relation do x and y satisfy?
quiz.explain: Setting PA² = PB² and cancelling x² and y² gives 4x + 8y = 36, so x + 2y = 9.
quiz.mistake: Makes a sign error when expanding the brackets

quiz.q: Which point is equidistant from A(2, 1) and B(4, 5)?
quiz.explain: (5, 2) satisfies x + 2y = 9 (5 + 4 = 9). Check: PA² = 9 + 1 = 10 and PB² = 1 + 9 = 10.
quiz.mistake: Picks a point that is near both but not equally far

quiz.q: Four friends sit at A(2, 3), B(5, 6), C(8, 3) and D(5, 0). What is the length AB?
quiz.mistake: Adds the gaps instead of squaring and adding

quiz.q: For the same friends at A(2, 3), B(5, 6), C(8, 3), D(5, 0), how long are the diagonals AC and BD?
quiz.explain: AC: same y, so 8 − 2 = 6. BD: same x, so 6 − 0 = 6. The diagonals are equal.
quiz.mistake: Uses a side length instead of a diagonal

quiz.q: Meera says the friends at A(2, 3), B(5, 6), C(8, 3), D(5, 0) form just a rhombus, not a square. Is she right?
options: Yes, because the sides are not equal
Yes, because the diagonals are unequal
No — all four sides are 3√2 and both diagonals are 6, so it is a square
quiz.explain: Equal sides make it at least a rhombus; equal diagonals as well make it a square.
quiz.mistake: Stops after checking the sides

quiz.q: Which point on the x-axis is equidistant from A(2, 1) and B(4, 5)?
quiz.explain: On the x-axis y = 0. Put y = 0 in x + 2y = 9: x = 9. Check: PA² = 49 + 1 = 50 and PB² = 25 + 25 = 50.
quiz.mistake: Takes the midpoint of the x-coordinates instead of using the relation

quiz.q: P(x, y) is equidistant from (0, 0) and (4, 0). What relation must hold?
quiz.explain: x² + y² = (x − 4)² + y² → 0 = −8x + 16 → x = 2. It is the vertical line through the midpoint.
quiz.mistake: Thinks y must be fixed instead of x

quiz.q: Benches are placed at (0, 0), (4, 0), (4, 3) and (0, 3). What shape do they form?
options: Rectangle that is not a square
quiz.explain: Opposite sides are 4 and 3 (not all equal) and both diagonals are 5. So it is a rectangle, not a square.
quiz.mistake: Sees equal diagonals and assumes a square

teach.ask: Gappu's four friends are sitting in class. How can he use coordinates to check if they form a square?
teach.praise: Tweet! All four sides equal AND both diagonals equal — then it's a square!
teach.nudge: Is checking only the four sides enough?

learn.hook: Want the exact spot one-third of the way from your home to school? The section formula pins it down!
points: The point P that divides the segment from A(x₁, y₁) to B(x₂, y₂) internally in the ratio m₁ : m₂ is P = ((m₁x₂ + m₂x₁)/(m₁ + m₂), (m₁y₂ + m₂y₁)/(m₁ + m₂)).
Remember: m₁ goes with the far end B, and m₂ with the near end A.
Midpoint (ratio 1 : 1): ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2).
To find an unknown ratio, call it k : 1 and solve for k.
Points of trisection divide a segment in the ratios 1 : 2 and 2 : 1.

example.q: Find the point that divides the join of A(−2, 5) and B(8, −5) in the ratio 2 : 3.

learn.reallife: Placing a water tank at a fair point between two villages, or a fielder between two cricket players, uses the section formula idea.

quiz.mistake: Forgets to halve the sum

quiz.q: One end of a diameter of a circle is (4, −1) and the centre is (1, 2). What is the other end?

topics.title: Equal parts, parallelograms, sports day — and chapter recap

learn.hook: Plant flags on a sports ground, find a lost corner of a parallelogram, and cut a road into four equal parts — all with the section formula!
points: To divide AB into four equal parts, find the points that divide it in 1 : 3, 1 : 1 and 3 : 1. The middle one is just the midpoint.
The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other: the midpoint of AC equals the midpoint of BD. Use this to find a missing vertex.
Story problems: turn positions into coordinates (line number, distance along it), then use the distance and midpoint formulas.
Recap: distance = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²]; distance from origin = √(x² + y²); section point = ((m₁x₂ + m₂x₁)/(m₁ + m₂), (m₁y₂ + m₂y₁)/(m₁ + m₂)); midpoint = ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2).

example.q: A(1, 1), B(5, 2) and C(6, 5) are three vertices of parallelogram ABCD. Find D.
steps: Diagonals AC and BD bisect each other

learn.reallife: Sports teachers mark lanes and flag positions on a grid; town planners split a road into equal stretches for street lights.

items.q: x of point 1/4 of the way from x = 1 to x = 9
x of D if A(1,1), B(5,2), C(6,5) form parallelogram ABCD

quiz.explain: Each quarter moves (9 − 1)/4 = 2 in x and (6 − (−2))/4 = 2 in y. So the points are (3, 0), (5, 2) and (7, 4).

quiz.q: A(1, 1), B(5, 2) and C(6, 5) are three vertices of parallelogram ABCD, in order. What is D?

quiz.q: In the parallelogram A(1, 1), B(5, 2), C(6, 5), D(2, 4), where do the diagonals meet?

quiz.q: On sports day, lines are drawn 1 m apart. Asha runs 20 m along the 3rd line and plants a flag at (3, 20). Bilal runs 30 m along the 7th line and plants a flag at (7, 30). How far apart are the flags?

quiz.q: Chetan wants to plant a flag exactly halfway between the flags at (3, 20) and (7, 30). Where should he put it?

quiz.q: Recap: how far is (−8, 6) from the origin?

quiz.q: Recap: which point divides the segment from A(2, 4) to B(8, 10) in the ratio 2 : 1?

quiz.mistake: Pairs m₁ with A instead of B, giving the 1 : 2 point

teach.ask: Gappu lost the fourth corner D of parallelogram ABCD. He knows A, B and C. How can he find D?
teach.praise: Chirp! The diagonals bisect each other, so the midpoints of AC and BD are the same — and that gives D!

learn.hook: How tall is that temple tower? How wide is that river? Trigonometry answers without a single climb or swim!
points: Trigonometry means 'measuring triangles' (from Greek words for three angles and measure). It links the sides and angles of a triangle.
It helps find heights and distances we cannot measure directly — a tower, the width of a river, how far a ship is from a lighthouse.
In Class 10 we study only acute angles in right-angled triangles.
sin A is ONE symbol: the sine of angle A. It is not 'sin × A', and you cannot cancel 'sin'.
sin²A means (sin A)², the square of sin A — not sin(A²).

example.q: If sin A = 3/5, find sin²A. Is it the same as sin(A²)?
steps: sin(A²) would mean the sine of the angle A², a completely different thing

learn.reallife: Surveyors, pilots, architects and astronomers use trigonometry daily — even your phone uses it to work out which way is up!

quiz.explain: sin A is a single symbol for a ratio linked to angle A. 'sin' on its own has no meaning.
quiz.mistake: Treats sin as a number that multiplies A

quiz.q: What does sin²A mean?
quiz.explain: The power 2 is on the value of sin A: sin²A = (sin A) × (sin A).
quiz.mistake: Puts the square on the angle instead of on the ratio

quiz.q: If sin A = 3/5, what is sin²A?
quiz.mistake: Doubles instead of squaring, or squares only the top

quiz.q: Rohan cancels 'sin' in sin 60°/sin 30° and writes 60/30 = 2. What is the true value?
quiz.explain: sin 60° = √3/2 and sin 30° = 1/2, so the ratio is (√3/2) ÷ (1/2) = √3. You cannot cancel 'sin'.
quiz.mistake: Cancels sin as if it were a number

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a typical use of trigonometry?
options: Finding the width of a river
Finding how far a ship is from a lighthouse
Finding how many sweets are in a box
Finding the angle at which a balcony looks down on a road
quiz.explain: Trigonometry deals with lengths and angles; counting sweets is not about triangles.
quiz.mistake: Thinks trigonometry is used for all kinds of counting

teach.ask: Gappu writes sin A as 'sin × A' and thinks he can cancel sin. Explain what trigonometry is and what sin A really means.
teach.praise: Chirp! sin A is one symbol for a ratio of sides — no cancelling sin!
teach.nudge: Is sin A a multiplication, or something else?

learn.hook: Three sides, one angle, six magic ratios — trigonometry is the secret language of right triangles!
points: In right ΔABC with ∠B = 90°, for the acute angle A: the side opposite A is BC, the side adjacent to A is AB, and AC is the hypotenuse.
sin A = opposite/hypotenuse, cos A = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan A = opposite/adjacent.
The reciprocals are cosec A = 1/sin A, sec A = 1/cos A and cot A = 1/tan A. Also tan A = sin A/cos A.
The ratios depend only on the angle, not on the size of the triangle.
For an acute angle, sin A and cos A are always less than 1, because the hypotenuse is the longest side. tan A can be any positive number.

example.q: If sin A = 3/5 for an acute angle A, find cos A and tan A.

learn.reallife: Ramp builders and roof makers use tan to set the right slope, so wheelchairs and rainwater both roll down safely.

games.title: Ratio reality check
items: sin A can be equal to 4/3 for an acute angle A.
sin A = opposite/hypotenuse, and the hypotenuse is the longest side, so sin A < 1.
tan A can be greater than 1.
tan A = opposite/adjacent, and the opposite side can be longer than the adjacent side.
cos A is short for cosecant A.
cos A is cosine A. Cosecant is written cosec A.
If a right triangle is enlarged to double size, sin A stays the same.
Both sides double, so their ratio does not change.
sec A = 1/cos A.
Secant is the reciprocal of cosine.
sin A means sin multiplied by A.
sin A is one symbol: the sine of the angle A.

quiz.q: In right ΔPQR, ∠Q = 90°, PQ = 5, QR = 12 and PR = 13. What is sin R?
quiz.explain: For ∠R, the opposite side is PQ = 5 and the hypotenuse is PR = 13. sin R = 5/13.
quiz.mistake: Uses the side next to R instead of the side opposite it

quiz.q: If tan A = 8/15, what is sin A?
quiz.explain: Take opposite = 8, adjacent = 15. Hypotenuse = √(64 + 225) = 17. sin A = 8/17.
quiz.mistake: Uses the adjacent side instead of the opposite side

quiz.q: If cos θ = 0.6, what is sec θ?
quiz.mistake: Thinks sec θ equals sin θ (4/5)

quiz.q: Which value can sin A NOT take for an acute angle A?
quiz.explain: sin A = opposite/hypotenuse, and the hypotenuse is the longest side, so sin A cannot be more than 1.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the hypotenuse is the longest side

quiz.q: In ΔABC, right-angled at B, AB = 24 cm and BC = 7 cm. What is cos A?
quiz.explain: AC = √(576 + 49) = 25. For ∠A, adjacent = AB = 24, so cos A = 24/25.
quiz.mistake: Uses the opposite side BC instead of the adjacent side

quiz.q: If 3 cot A = 4, what is tan A?
quiz.explain: cot A = 4/3, and tan A = 1/cot A = 3/4.
quiz.mistake: Thinks tan A and cot A are equal

quiz.q: A 5 m ladder leans against a wall with its foot 3 m from the wall. What is the cosine of the angle it makes with the ground?
quiz.explain: For the angle at the ground, the adjacent side is 3 m and the hypotenuse (the ladder) is 5 m. cos = 3/5.
quiz.mistake: Uses the height on the wall (4 m) instead of the distance on the ground

quiz.q: Kabir says sin 30° is bigger in a big triangle than in a small one. Is he right?
options: No, trigonometric ratios depend only on the angle
Yes, bigger triangles have bigger ratios
Yes, because the hypotenuse is longer
No, sin 30° is smaller in a big triangle
quiz.explain: Right triangles with the same acute angle are similar, so their sides are in the same ratio. sin 30° is always 1/2.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the ratio depends on the length of the sides

teach.ask: Gappu points at a right triangle: 'What do sin, cos and tan actually mean?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Opposite over hypotenuse, adjacent over hypotenuse, opposite over adjacent. SOH-CAH-TOA!
teach.nudge: Which sides of the triangle do I divide for sin, for cos and for tan?

topics.title: All six ratios and evaluating expressions

learn.hook: Know one ratio and Pythagoras, and you can unlock all six — then crack any expression thrown at you!
points: From the three sides, write all six: sin = opp/hyp, cos = adj/hyp, tan = opp/adj, and their flips cosec, sec, cot.
Given one ratio, draw a right triangle with those two sides, find the third side by Pythagoras, then read off the rest.
To evaluate an expression like (4 sin A − cos A)/(4 sin A + cos A), substitute the values — or divide top and bottom by cos A to use tan A directly.
True/false checks: sin A and cos A are never more than 1 (for acute A); sec A and cosec A are never less than 1; tan A and cot A can be any positive value.

example.q: In ΔABC, right-angled at B, AB = 8 cm, BC = 6 cm and AC = 10 cm. Write all six ratios of angle A.
steps: Opposite A = BC = 6, adjacent = AB = 8, hypotenuse = AC = 10
cosec A = 5/3, sec A = 5/4, cot A = 4/3
example.answer: sin 3/5, cos 4/5, tan 3/4, cosec 5/3, sec 5/4, cot 4/3

learn.reallife: A carpenter making a slanting roof checks the slope (tan) and the beam length (sec) from just one measured angle.

games.title: Possible or impossible? (A is acute)
items: tan A = 5/2 is possible.
tan A can be any positive number.
sin A = 4/3 is possible.
sin A ≤ 1 because the hypotenuse is the longest side.
sec A = 12/5 is possible.
sec A ≥ 1, and 12/5 > 1.
cos A = 1.2 is possible.
cos A cannot exceed 1.
cot A is the product of cot and A.
cot A is one symbol, the cotangent of A.
tan A is always less than 1.

quiz.q: In ΔABC, right-angled at B, AB = 8 cm, BC = 6 cm and AC = 10 cm. What is cosec A?
quiz.explain: cosec A = hypotenuse/opposite = 10/6 = 5/3.
quiz.mistake: Uses the adjacent side instead of the opposite side

quiz.q: In the same triangle (AB = 8, BC = 6, AC = 10, right angle at B), what is cot A?
quiz.explain: cot A = adjacent/opposite = AB/BC = 8/6 = 4/3.
quiz.mistake: Writes tan A instead of cot A

quiz.q: If cot θ = 5/12, what is (1 + sin θ)(1 − sin θ) ÷ [(1 + cos θ)(1 − cos θ)]?
quiz.explain: The top is 1 − sin²θ = cos²θ and the bottom is 1 − cos²θ = sin²θ, so the expression is cot²θ = 25/144.
steps: (1 + sin θ)(1 − sin θ) = 1 − sin²θ = cos²θ
quiz.mistake: Uses tan²θ instead of cot²θ

quiz.q: If 4 tan A = 3, what is (4 sin A − cos A)/(4 sin A + cos A)?
quiz.explain: Divide top and bottom by cos A: (4 tan A − 1)/(4 tan A + 1) = (3 − 1)/(3 + 1) = 1/2.
quiz.mistake: Puts tan A = 3 instead of 4 tan A = 3

quiz.q: For an acute angle A, which statement is true?
options: sec A = 12/5 for some value of A
quiz.explain: sec A is always at least 1, and 12/5 > 1, so it is possible. tan can exceed 1, cos A is one symbol, and sin can't exceed 1.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all six ratios must be less than 1

quiz.q: If sin A = 12/13 and A is acute, what is sec A?
quiz.explain: The adjacent side = √(13² − 12²) = 5, so cos A = 5/13 and sec A = 13/5.
quiz.mistake: Flips sin instead of cos (gets cosec A)

quiz.q: If sec θ = 13/12 and θ is acute, what is tan θ?
quiz.explain: cos θ = 12/13, so adjacent 12, hypotenuse 13 and opposite 5. tan θ = 5/12.
quiz.mistake: Divides adjacent by opposite

quiz.q: If tan A = 3/4 and A is acute, what is 2 sin A cos A?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the factor 2

teach.ask: Gappu knows only that tan A = 3/4. How can he find the other five ratios?
teach.praise: Tweet! Draw the triangle, get the third side by Pythagoras, then read off the rest and flip them!
teach.nudge: How does he find the missing third side?

topics.title: Where the values of 30°, 45° and 60° come from

learn.hook: Don't just memorise the table — rebuild it in 30 seconds from a half-square and a half-equilateral triangle!
points: 45°: take a right triangle with two equal legs a. The hypotenuse is a√2, so sin 45° = cos 45° = 1/√2 and tan 45° = 1.
30° and 60°: cut an equilateral triangle of side 2a by an altitude. You get a right triangle with sides a, a√3 and 2a, and angles 30°, 60°, 90°.
Warning: sin(A + B) is NOT sin A + sin B. With A = 30°, B = 60°: sin 90° = 1, but sin 30° + sin 60° = (1 + √3)/2.

example.q: Use an equilateral triangle of side 2 to find sin 30° and tan 60°.
steps: The altitude cuts the base into halves of 1 and makes angles of 30° at the top and 60° at the base

learn.reallife: Set squares in your geometry box are exactly these triangles: one 45°–45°–90° and one 30°–60°–90°!

games.title: Derive sin 30°
items: Draw an equilateral triangle ABC with side 2a
Drop the altitude AD to BC; BD = a
∠BAD = 30° and ∠ABD = 60°
AD = √(4a² − a²) = a√3
sin 30° = BD/AB = a/2a = 1/2

items.text: Isosceles right triangle with legs 1 has hypotenuse ___
Equilateral triangle of side 2 has altitude ___
tan 45° = ___ because the legs are equal

quiz.q: A right triangle has two equal legs of length 1. What is its hypotenuse?
quiz.explain: By Pythagoras, hyp² = 1² + 1² = 2, so the hypotenuse is √2.
quiz.mistake: Adds the legs instead of using Pythagoras

quiz.q: Using that triangle (legs 1, hypotenuse √2), what is sin 45°?
quiz.explain: sin 45° = opposite/hypotenuse = 1/√2.
quiz.mistake: Divides hypotenuse by opposite

quiz.q: An equilateral triangle of side 2 is cut by an altitude. How long is the altitude?
quiz.explain: Half the base is 1, so altitude = √(2² − 1²) = √3.
quiz.mistake: Adds squares instead of subtracting

quiz.q: In the half-triangle with sides 1, √3 and 2, which angle is opposite the side of length 1?
quiz.explain: The smallest side is opposite the smallest angle. The angles are 30°, 60° and 90°, so it is 30°.
steps: Shortest side faces the smallest angle
quiz.mistake: Matches the shortest side with 60°

quiz.q: From the same half-triangle, what is tan 60°?
quiz.explain: For 60°, the opposite side is √3 and the adjacent side is 1, so tan 60° = √3.
quiz.mistake: Uses 30° by mistake and gets 1/√3

quiz.q: Take A = 30° and B = 60°. Which statement is true?
options: sin(A + B) = 1, but sin A + sin B = (1 + √3)/2, so they are not equal
sin(A + B) = sin A + sin B
quiz.mistake: Thinks sin can be 'opened up' like a bracket

quiz.q: Is cos(60° − 30°) equal to cos 60° − cos 30°?
quiz.explain: cos(60° − 30°) = cos 30° = √3/2, while cos 60° − cos 30° = 1/2 − √3/2, which is negative.
quiz.mistake: Distributes cos over subtraction

quiz.q: Why is tan 45° = 1?
options: Because in a 45°–45°–90° triangle the opposite and adjacent sides are equal
quiz.explain: tan = opposite/adjacent, and the two legs are equal in an isosceles right triangle, so the ratio is 1.
quiz.mistake: Thinks sin 45° itself equals 1

teach.ask: Gappu forgot the value of sin 30°. Show him how to rebuild it from an equilateral triangle.
teach.praise: Chirp! Cut an equilateral triangle in half — the side opposite 30° is half the hypotenuse, so sin 30° = 1/2!
teach.nudge: What happens to the base when you draw the altitude?

learn.hook: Five special angles — 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90° — have values every board exam expects you to know by heart!
points: cos runs the other way: cos 0° = 1, cos 30° = √3/2, cos 45° = 1/√2, cos 60° = 1/2, cos 90° = 0.
tan 0° = 0, tan 30° = 1/√3, tan 45° = 1, tan 60° = √3, and tan 90° is not defined.
These come from an equilateral triangle (for 30° and 60°) and an isosceles right triangle (for 45°).
As A increases from 0° to 90°, sin A increases from 0 to 1 and cos A decreases from 1 to 0.

example.q: Evaluate sin 60° cos 30° + sin 30° cos 60°.

learn.reallife: Set squares in your geometry box have angles 30°, 45°, 60° and 90° — exactly the standard angles!

quiz.q: What is sin 60° × cos 30°?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to square the √3 or the 2

quiz.q: What is 2 tan 45° + cos² 60°?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to square cos 60° and adds 1/2

quiz.q: If sin A = 1/2 and A is acute, what is A?
quiz.mistake: Mixes up sin 30° with cos 30° and answers 60°

quiz.q: If sin(A + B) = 1 and cos(A − B) = √3/2, where A and B are acute and A > B, what is A?
quiz.mistake: Gives B (30°) instead of A

quiz.q: Which of these is not defined?
quiz.explain: tan 90° = sin 90°/cos 90° = 1/0, and division by zero is not defined.
quiz.mistake: Thinks cos 90° = 0 means it is undefined

quiz.q: What is (1 − tan² 45°)/(1 + tan² 45°)?
quiz.mistake: Uses tan 45° = 0 by mistake

quiz.q: As angle A increases from 0° to 90°, what happens to cos A?
quiz.explain: cos 0° = 1 and cos 90° = 0, and cos A falls steadily in between.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the behaviour of cos A with sin A

quiz.q: In ΔABC, right-angled at B, ∠A = 30° and AC = 10 cm. What is BC?
quiz.explain: BC is opposite ∠A, so sin 30° = BC/AC. BC = 10 × 1/2 = 5 cm.
quiz.mistake: Uses cos 30° and gets 5√3 cm, which is AB

teach.ask: Gappu forgot his table: 'How can I remember sin of 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°?'
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! sin goes 0, 1/2, 1/√2, √3/2, 1 — and cos is the same list backwards!
teach.nudge: What is sin 30°, and what are the values at 0° and 90°?

learn.hook: Some trig equations are true for EVERY angle — these identities are your shortcuts for proofs!
points: sin²A + cos²A = 1 for every angle A from 0° to 90°. It comes from Pythagoras: divide (opp² + adj² = hyp²) by hyp².
Divide by cos²A: 1 + tan²A = sec²A (for 0° ≤ A < 90°).
Divide by sin²A: 1 + cot²A = cosec²A (for 0° < A ≤ 90°).
Use them to find all the other ratios when one ratio is known.
To prove an identity, start from the harder side and simplify it into the other side.

example.q: If sin A = 5/13 and A is acute, find sec A.
steps: cos A = 12/13 (A is acute, so positive)

learn.reallife: Sound engineers and phone signal designers rely on sin² + cos² = 1 when they mix and split waves.

items.text: sin²A + ___ = 1
1 + tan²A = ___
cosec²A − cot²A = ___
(1 − sin²A) sec²A = ___
sec²A − 1 = ___

games.title: Identity or impostor?
items: sin²A + cos²A = 1 for every angle A from 0° to 90°.
It follows from Pythagoras theorem.
sec²A − tan²A = 1.
Rearrange 1 + tan²A = sec²A.
sin A + cos A = 1 for every angle A.
At 45°, sin A + cos A = 2/√2 = √2, which is not 1.
1 + cot²A = sec²A.
The correct identity is 1 + cot²A = cosec²A.
(sec A − tan A)(sec A + tan A) = 1.
It equals sec²A − tan²A = 1.
tan²A − sec²A = 1.
tan²A − sec²A = −1.

quiz.q: Simplify (1 + tan²A) cos²A.
quiz.explain: 1 + tan²A = sec²A, and sec²A × cos²A = 1.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies only the 1 by cos²A

quiz.q: If cos A = 8/17 and A is acute, what is sin A?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts without squaring: 17 − 8 = 9

quiz.q: What is 9 sec²A − 9 tan²A?
quiz.explain: 9(sec²A − tan²A) = 9 × 1 = 9.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the factor 9 and writes 1

quiz.q: If sec θ + tan θ = 4, what is sec θ − tan θ?
quiz.explain: (sec θ + tan θ)(sec θ − tan θ) = sec²θ − tan²θ = 1, so sec θ − tan θ = 1/4.
steps: (sec θ + tan θ)(sec θ − tan θ) = 1
quiz.mistake: Thinks the two expressions are equal or just opposite in sign

quiz.q: If sin A = 7/25 and A is acute, what is tan A?
quiz.mistake: Writes tan A = cos A/sin A (24/7)

quiz.q: Simplify (1 + cot²A) sin²A.
quiz.explain: 1 + cot²A = cosec²A, and cosec²A × sin²A = 1.
quiz.mistake: Uses 1 + cot²A = sec²A by mistake

quiz.q: Which expression is equal to cos²A?
quiz.explain: From sin²A + cos²A = 1, cos²A = 1 − sin²A.
quiz.mistake: Gets the sign the wrong way round when rearranging

quiz.q: What is sin² 30° + cos² 30°?
quiz.explain: (1/2)² + (√3/2)² = 1/4 + 3/4 = 1, as the identity promises.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to square the values

teach.ask: Gappu heard sin²A + cos²A = 1 works for every angle: 'Why is that true?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Pythagoras divided by hypotenuse squared — so sin² plus cos² is always 1. Mind blown!
teach.nudge: Which famous theorem about right triangles is hiding inside this identity?

learn.hook: An identity is a promise that works for EVERY angle. Proving one is like solving a puzzle: transform one side until it matches the other!
points: An identity is an equation that is true for ALL values of the angle for which both sides are defined. sin A = cos A is NOT an identity (true only at 45°).
To prove LHS = RHS: start with the more complicated side, change everything to sin and cos if stuck, simplify, and reach the other side.
Useful tools: sin²A + cos²A = 1, sec²A − tan²A = 1, cosec²A − cot²A = 1, and common denominators.
Recap: six ratios and their reciprocals; standard values for 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°; the three identities.

example.q: Prove that (1 + tan²A)/(1 + cot²A) = tan²A.
steps: LHS = sec²A / cosec²A (using the two identities)

learn.reallife: Engineers simplify long trigonometric expressions with identities before computing — fewer steps, fewer mistakes.

games.title: Match the expression to its simplest form
pairs: cos A/(1 − sin A) − cos A/(1 + sin A)

games.title: Identity or not?
items: sin²A + cos²A = 1 is an identity.
It holds for every angle A.
sin A = cos A is an identity.
It is true only when A = 45°.
1 + tan²A = sec²A is an identity (A ≠ 90°).
It comes from dividing sin²A + cos²A = 1 by cos²A.
To prove an identity you may assume it is true and work both sides at once.
Start from one side and transform it into the other.
sec A − tan A = 1/(sec A + tan A).
Because (sec A − tan A)(sec A + tan A) = sec²A − tan²A = 1.

quiz.q: What makes an equation an identity?
options: It is true for one special angle
It is true for all values of the angle for which both sides are defined
It contains only sin and cos
It has no numbers in it
quiz.explain: An identity holds for every value of the angle (where defined), not just for some angles.
quiz.mistake: Thinks an equation that works for one angle is an identity

quiz.q: Is sin A = cos A an identity?
options: Yes, because both are less than 1
No — it is true only when A = 45°
quiz.explain: At 45° both are 1/√2, but at 30° sin = 1/2 and cos = √3/2. So it is not true for all A.
quiz.mistake: Generalises from one angle

quiz.q: To prove (sec A − tan A)(sec A + tan A) = 1, which identity do you use?
quiz.explain: The left side is a difference of squares: sec²A − tan²A, which equals 1 since 1 + tan²A = sec²A.
quiz.mistake: Picks the identity with the wrong pair of ratios

quiz.q: Simplify (1 − cos²A) cosec²A.
quiz.explain: 1 − cos²A = sin²A, and sin²A × cosec²A = sin²A × 1/sin²A = 1.
quiz.mistake: Stops at sin²A and forgets the cosec²A

quiz.q: Which expression equals tan A + cot A?
quiz.explain: sin/cos + cos/sin = (sin² + cos²)/(sin cos) = 1/(sin A cos A) = sec A cosec A.
quiz.mistake: Adds the reciprocals wrongly

quiz.q: Simplify cos A/(1 − sin A) − cos A/(1 + sin A).
quiz.explain: Common denominator 1 − sin²A = cos²A. Top: cos A(1 + sin A) − cos A(1 − sin A) = 2 sin A cos A. So the result is 2 sin A cos A/cos²A = 2 tan A.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the denominators directly

quiz.q: Evaluate 6 cosec²θ − 6 cot²θ.
quiz.explain: 6(cosec²θ − cot²θ) = 6 × 1 = 6.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the expression is always 0 or 1

quiz.q: Which is the correct proof of (1 + tan²A)/(1 + cot²A) = tan²A?
options: Cancel the 1s to get tan²A/cot²A = tan²A
quiz.explain: Use 1 + tan²A = sec²A and 1 + cot²A = cosec²A, then flip: sin²A/cos²A = tan²A. Checking one angle is not a proof.
quiz.mistake: Thinks checking one angle proves an identity

quiz.q: Recap: what is sec 60°?
quiz.mistake: Gives cos 60° instead of its reciprocal

teach.ask: Gappu checked sin²A + cos²A = 1 for A = 30° and says it's proved. Explain what an identity is and how to really prove one.
teach.praise: Tweet! One angle is just a check — a proof works for every angle by turning one side into the other!
teach.nudge: Does checking just one angle prove it for every angle?

learn.hook: Look up at a kite or down from a balcony — the angle your eyes turn through is the key to measuring things you can't reach!
points: The line of sight is the straight line from your eye to the object you are looking at.
Angle of elevation: the angle between the horizontal and the line of sight when you look UP at an object.
Angle of depression: the angle between the horizontal and the line of sight when you look DOWN at an object.
The angle of elevation of A from B equals the angle of depression of B from A — they are alternate angles between parallel horizontal lines.
As you walk towards a tower, the angle of elevation of its top increases. If the height equals the distance, the angle is 45°.

example.q: A kite is flying on a 100 m string that makes an angle of 30° with the ground. How high is the kite? (Assume the string is straight.)
steps: The string is the hypotenuse; the height is opposite the 30° angle

learn.reallife: During Makar Sankranti, kite flyers can estimate how high their kite is from the string length and the angle it makes with the ground.

games.title: Elevation or depression?
items: Arjun on the ground looks up at a kite
A pilot looks down at the runway
Meena on a balcony looks at a car below
A boy on the ground looks at the top of a temple
A lighthouse keeper looks at a boat at sea
A cricketer looks up at a ball high in the air
From a hilltop, Aisha looks at a village below

games.title: Line-of-sight check
items: The angle of elevation is measured from the horizontal.
It is the angle between the horizontal line and the line of sight.
The angle of depression of a point P from the top of a tower equals the angle of elevation of the top from P.
They are alternate angles between parallel horizontal lines.
As you walk towards a tower, the angle of elevation of its top decreases.
It increases — the top looks steeper as you get closer.
If a tower's height equals your distance from its foot, the angle of elevation is 45°.
tan θ = height/distance = 1, so θ = 45°.
The angle of depression is measured from the vertical line.
It is measured down from the horizontal line.
A longer shadow of the same pole means the sun is lower in the sky.
A smaller angle of elevation of the sun gives a longer shadow.

quiz.q: A tower's height equals the distance of a point from its foot. What is the angle of elevation of the top from that point?
quiz.explain: tan θ = height/distance = 1, so θ = 45°.
quiz.mistake: Thinks equal sides give 60° as in an equilateral triangle

quiz.q: A kite flies on a 60 m string at an angle of elevation of 30°. How high is it?
quiz.explain: sin 30° = height/60, so height = 60 × 1/2 = 30 m.
quiz.mistake: Uses cos 30° and gets 30√3 m

quiz.q: A 10 m pole casts a shadow 10√3 m long. What is the sun's angle of elevation?
quiz.mistake: Computes shadow/height and gets 60°

quiz.mistake: Mixes up alternate and vertically opposite angles

quiz.q: The sun's angle of elevation rises from 30° to 60°. What happens to the shadow of a flagpole?
quiz.explain: shadow = height/tan θ. tan 60° is bigger than tan 30°, so the shadow gets shorter.

topics.title: Poles across a road, balloons, birds — and chapter recap

learn.hook: A bird flies off a treetop, a balloon drifts in the wind, two poles face each other across a road — one ratio, tan, solves them all!
points: Two poles across a road: let the unknown distance from one pole be x; the other is (width − x). Write tan for each triangle with the same height h and solve.
Moving objects at a fixed height (a bird flying level, a drifting balloon): find the horizontal distance at each angle and subtract. Speed = distance ÷ time.
Ropes and ladders are slant lengths, so use sin (height = rope × sin θ) or cos (ground distance = rope × cos θ).
In Class 10 problems, angles are only 30°, 45° and 60°, and at most two right triangles are used. Use √3 ≈ 1.732 when asked for a decimal.
Recap: line of sight; angle of elevation (looking up) and depression (looking down) are equal for the same pair of points; choose the ratio that links the known and unknown sides.

example.q: Two poles of equal height stand on opposite sides of a road 100 m wide. From a point on the road between them, the angles of elevation of their tops are 60° and 30°. Find the height of the poles.
steps: Let the point be x m from the first pole (60°), so (100 − x) m from the other (30°)
example.answer: Each pole is 25√3 m ≈ 43.3 m high

learn.reallife: Traffic engineers place street lights on both sides of a road at heights that light up the middle — the same two-triangle problem!

quiz.explain: h = √3x and h = (100 − x)/√3 give 3x = 100 − x, so x = 25 and h = 25√3 m.

quiz.q: In the same problem, how far is the point from the pole whose top is seen at 60°?
quiz.explain: From 3x = 100 − x, x = 25 m. The point is closer to the pole seen at the larger angle.

quiz.q: Riya's eyes are 1.5 m above the ground. A balloon flying at 51.5 m is first seen at 45° elevation and, after drifting level, at 30°. Using √3 = 1.732, how far did it drift?
quiz.explain: Height above her eyes = 50 m. Distances: 50/tan 45° = 50 m and 50/tan 30° = 50√3 ≈ 86.6 m. Drift ≈ 86.6 − 50 = 36.6 m.

quiz.q: A bird sits on top of a 20 m tree; from a point on the ground its angle of elevation is 45°. It flies away level, and 2 seconds later the angle is 30°. Using √3 = 1.732, what is the bird's speed in m/s?
quiz.explain: Distances: 20 m (at 45°) and 20√3 ≈ 34.64 m (at 30°). It flew 14.64 m in 2 s, so the speed is 7.32 m/s.
quiz.mistake: Gives the distance flown instead of dividing by the time

quiz.q: A 16 m rope is stretched tight from the top of a vertical pole to the ground, making 30° with the ground. How tall is the pole?
quiz.explain: The rope is the hypotenuse, so height = 16 × sin 30° = 16 × 1/2 = 8 m.
quiz.mistake: Uses cos or tan instead of sin

quiz.q: In Class 10 heights-and-distances problems, which angles of elevation or depression are used?
quiz.explain: The syllabus restricts problems to 30°, 45° and 60°, with at most two right triangles.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any angle may appear

quiz.q: From the top of a 12 m building, the angle of elevation of the top of a taller building across the road is 30°, and the angle of depression of its foot is 45°. Using √3 = 1.732, how tall is the taller building?
quiz.explain: 45° depression → road width = 12 m. Extra height above 12 m = 12 tan 30° = 12/√3 ≈ 6.93 m. Total ≈ 18.93 m.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to add the height of the first building

quiz.q: A 6 m pole and a 10 m pole stand 4 m apart on level ground. What is the angle of elevation of the top of the taller pole from the top of the shorter one?
quiz.explain: The height difference is 10 − 6 = 4 m and the gap is 4 m, so tan θ = 4/4 = 1 and θ = 45°.
quiz.mistake: Uses the full height 10 m instead of the difference

teach.ask: Gappu sees two equal poles across a road and wants their height. He knows the road width and both angles. Explain how to set it up.
teach.praise: Chirp! Split the road into x and (width − x), write tan for each side with the same h, and solve!
teach.nudge: What is the same in both triangles?

topics.title: Circle basics and how a tangent is born

learn.hook: Slide two points of a cutting line closer and closer together… and the moment they meet, a tangent is born!
points: A circle is the set of all points at a fixed distance (the radius) from a fixed point (the centre). A chord joins two points of the circle; the diameter is the longest chord. An arc is a part of the circle.
A line and a circle can have 0 common points (non-intersecting), 2 (a secant) or exactly 1 (a tangent).
Compare the distance d of the line from the centre with the radius r: d > r → no common point; d = r → tangent; d < r → secant.

Activity: pin a straight wire at a point P on a circle and rotate it. It cuts the circle at a second point in every position except ONE — that position is the tangent at P. So there is exactly one tangent at each point.
Limiting case: if a secant cuts the circle at P and Q, and Q slides towards P, the chord PQ shrinks to zero and the secant becomes the tangent at P.

example.q: A secant cuts a circle at P and Q. What happens as Q moves along the circle towards P?
steps: The chord PQ gets shorter and shorter
When Q reaches P, the two common points become one
The secant has turned into the tangent at P
example.answer: The secant becomes the tangent at P

learn.reallife: A bicycle wheel touching the road, a ball resting on the floor — the ground is a tangent, touching at just one point.

quiz.mistake: Confuses chords with radii or tangents

quiz.q: What is an arc?
options: A part of the circle between two of its points
quiz.explain: An arc is a piece of the circle (the curved boundary) between two points on it.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up arc with chord or sector

quiz.q: A straight wire is pinned at point P on a circle and rotated. In how many positions does it meet the circle ONLY at P?
quiz.explain: In every other position the wire cuts the circle again. Only one position touches at P alone: the tangent at P.

quiz.q: A secant cuts a circle at P and Q. As Q slides along the circle towards P, what does the secant become?

quiz.mistake: Does not see the tangent as the limiting position of a secant

quiz.q: A line is 3 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm. What is the line?
options: It does not meet the circle
quiz.explain: 3 < 5, so the line passes inside the circle and cuts it at two points: a secant.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any line not through the centre is a tangent

quiz.q: How many points does a tangent have in common with its circle?
quiz.explain: A tangent touches the circle at exactly one point, the point of contact.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a tangent with a secant

quiz.q: A line is 6 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm. What can you say?
options: It does not meet the circle
quiz.explain: 6 > 5, so every point of the line is outside the circle: the line and the circle have no common point.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every line near a circle must touch it

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How can a line that cuts a circle twice turn into a tangent?' Explain using the secant idea.
teach.praise: Chirp! Slide the second point onto the first — two meeting points become one, and the secant becomes a tangent!
teach.nudge: What happens to the two points where the secant meets the circle?

learn.hook: A bicycle wheel touches the road at just ONE point — that road is a tangent to the wheel!
points: A secant is a line that meets a circle at two points. A tangent meets it at exactly one point, called the point of contact.
A circle has infinitely many tangents — one at every point on it.
From a point inside the circle there is no tangent, from a point on the circle exactly one, and from a point outside exactly two.
Theorem: the tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.
Tangents at the two ends of a diameter are parallel to each other.

example.q: A circle has radius 5 cm and a point P is 13 cm from its centre O. Find the length of the tangent from P.
steps: The radius OQ is perpendicular to the tangent PQ, so ΔOQP is right-angled at Q

learn.reallife: A car tyre touches the flat road at just one point, and a ruler laid against a bangle touches it at one point — the road and the ruler are tangents.

quiz.q: PQ touches a circle with centre O at Q, and ∠POQ = 60°. What is ∠OPQ?

quiz.mistake: Forgets that the angle between the tangent and the radius is 90°

quiz.q: How many tangents can a circle have?
quiz.explain: There is one tangent at every point of the circle, and a circle has infinitely many points.

quiz.q: What is a line that meets a circle at two points called?
quiz.explain: A secant cuts the circle at two points, while a tangent only touches it at one.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the words secant and tangent

quiz.q: A circle has radius 3 cm. Two parallel tangents are drawn to it. How far apart are they?
quiz.explain: Parallel tangents touch the circle at the ends of a diameter, so they are a diameter apart: 2 × 3 = 6 cm.
quiz.mistake: Uses the radius instead of the diameter

quiz.q: How many tangents can be drawn to a circle from a point inside it?
quiz.explain: Any line through an inside point crosses the circle at two points, so none of them is a tangent.
quiz.mistake: Thinks there is always at least one tangent

quiz.q: A bicycle wheel rests on a flat road. What angle does the spoke from the hub to the touching point make with the road?
quiz.explain: The road is a tangent to the wheel, and the spoke is a radius to the point of contact, so they are perpendicular.
quiz.mistake: Does not link the road to a tangent

teach.ask: Gappu rolls a bangle on the table: 'What is special about the table and the bangle's radius where they touch?'

learn.hook: From any point outside a circle, the two tangents you draw are always perfect twins — exactly the same length!
points: Theorem: the lengths of the two tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal: PA = PB.
Proof idea: ΔOAP and ΔOBP are right-angled at A and B, share the hypotenuse OP and have OA = OB, so they are congruent (RHS).
So OP bisects ∠APB, and ∠OPA = ∠OPB.
In quadrilateral OAPB, ∠A = ∠B = 90°, so ∠AOB + ∠APB = 180°.
Tangent length from P: PA = √(OP² − r²).

example.q: PA and PB are tangents from P to a circle with centre O, and ∠APB = 70°. Find ∠AOB and ∠OPA.

learn.reallife: A rope wrapped around a pulley from one fixed hook leaves the wheel along two equal tangent lengths.

quiz.q: PA and PB are tangents from P to a circle with centre O. If ∠APB = 80°, what is ∠AOB?
quiz.mistake: Thinks ∠AOB equals ∠APB

quiz.q: PA and PB are tangents with ∠APB = 80°. What is ∠AOP?
quiz.explain: OP bisects ∠APB, so ∠APO = 40°. In right ΔOAP, ∠AOP = 90° − 40° = 50°.
quiz.mistake: Gives ∠APO (40°) instead of ∠AOP

quiz.q: From P, the tangent PA to a circle is 12 cm long. How long is the other tangent PB?
quiz.explain: Tangents from an external point are equal, so PB = PA = 12 cm.
quiz.mistake: Thinks more information is needed

quiz.q: PA and PB are tangents from P with ∠PAB = 65°. What is ∠APB?
quiz.explain: PA = PB, so ΔPAB is isosceles and ∠PBA = 65°. Then ∠APB = 180° − 130° = 50°.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the base angles of the isosceles triangle are equal

quiz.q: Two tangents from P to a circle of radius 5 cm are inclined at 60°. What is OP?
quiz.explain: ∠OPA = 30° and ∠OAP = 90°. sin 30° = OA/OP, so OP = 5 ÷ 1/2 = 10 cm.
quiz.mistake: Uses the full 60° instead of half of it

quiz.q: Tangents PA and PB from P make ∠APB = 60° with a circle of radius 5 cm. How long is PA?
quiz.explain: In right ΔOAP, ∠OPA = 30°, so tan 30° = OA/PA and PA = 5 ÷ (1/√3) = 5√3 cm.
quiz.mistake: Uses tan 60° and gets 5/√3 cm

quiz.q: Why are the two tangents from an external point P equal?
options: Because all lines from P are equal
Because right triangles OAP and OBP are congruent by RHS
Because the angles at P are 90°
quiz.explain: OA = OB (radii), OP is common, and ∠OAP = ∠OBP = 90°. By RHS the triangles are congruent, so PA = PB.
quiz.mistake: Gives a reason without using the right angles at A and B

quiz.q: Two tangents from P to a circle of radius 4 cm meet at 90°. What shape is OAPB?
options: A rhombus with no right angle
quiz.explain: ∠A = ∠B = ∠P = 90°, so ∠O = 90° too. OA = OB = 4 and PA = PB; a rectangle with two adjacent sides equal (OA = PA = 4 cm) is a square.
quiz.mistake: Notices equal tangents but not the four right angles

teach.ask: Gappu draws two tangents from his perch to a round pond: 'Are these two tangents the same length? Why?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Equal radii, right angles and a shared side make congruent triangles — so the tangents are twins!

learn.hook: With the 'equal tangents' rule, puzzles about circles hiding inside triangles and squares become easy!
points: If a circle touches all four sides of quadrilateral ABCD, then AB + CD = AD + BC.
So a parallelogram that circumscribes a circle must be a rhombus.
In a triangle with an incircle, the two tangents from each vertex are equal, so each side splits into two known pieces.
For two concentric circles, a chord of the bigger circle that touches the smaller circle is bisected at the point of contact.
If TP and TQ are tangents from T, then ∠PTQ = 2∠OPQ.

example.q: A circle touches all four sides of ABCD. AB = 6 cm, BC = 7 cm and CD = 4 cm. Find AD.

Tangents from one point are equal: AP = AS, BP = BQ, CR = CQ, DR = DS
Add them: AP + BP + CR + DR = AS + BQ + CQ + DS
So AB + CD = AD + BC

quiz.q: Quadrilateral ABCD circumscribes a circle, with AB = 8 cm, BC = 10 cm and CD = 7 cm. What is AD?
quiz.explain: AB + CD = AD + BC, so 8 + 7 = AD + 10 and AD = 5 cm.
quiz.mistake: Pairs adjacent sides instead of opposite sides

quiz.q: Two concentric circles have radii 13 cm and 5 cm. A chord of the larger circle touches the smaller one. How long is the chord?
quiz.explain: The radius 5 cm meets the chord at 90° at its midpoint. Half-chord = √(169 − 25) = 12, so the chord is 24 cm.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to double the half-chord

quiz.q: The incircle of ΔABC touches AB at P, BC at Q and CA at R. AP = 4 cm, BQ = 6 cm and CR = 5 cm. What is the perimeter of ΔABC?
quiz.explain: Each tangent length appears twice: AP = AR, BP = BQ, CQ = CR. Perimeter = 2(4 + 6 + 5) = 30 cm.
quiz.mistake: Adds each tangent length only once

quiz.q: A parallelogram circumscribes a circle. What kind of parallelogram must it be?
quiz.explain: AB + CD = AD + BC with AB = CD and AD = BC gives 2AB = 2BC, so all sides are equal: a rhombus.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any parallelogram can hold a circle touching all sides

quiz.q: In ΔABC, AB = 10 cm, BC = 8 cm and CA = 12 cm. Its incircle touches AB at P. What is AP?
quiz.explain: Let AP = AR = x. Then BP = BQ = 10 − x and CR = CQ = 12 − x. BQ + CQ = 8 gives 22 − 2x = 8, so x = 7 cm.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the point of contact is the midpoint of AB

quiz.q: A rangoli circle is drawn inside a square frame of side 14 cm, touching all four sides. What is its radius?
quiz.explain: Opposite sides of the square are parallel tangents, so they are a diameter apart. Diameter = 14 cm, radius = 7 cm.
quiz.mistake: Takes the side of the square as the radius

quiz.q: TP and TQ are tangents from T to a circle with centre O, and ∠PTQ = 70°. What is ∠OPQ?
quiz.explain: ΔTPQ is isosceles, so ∠TPQ = (180° − 70°)/2 = 55°. ∠OPT = 90°, so ∠OPQ = 90° − 55° = 35° (half of 70°).
quiz.mistake: Gives ∠TPQ (55°) instead of ∠OPQ

quiz.q: A right triangle has legs 6 cm and 8 cm. What is the radius of its incircle?
quiz.explain: The hypotenuse is 10 cm. From the right-angle vertex both tangents equal r, so (6 − r) + (8 − r) = 10, giving r = 2 cm.
quiz.mistake: Halves a side instead of using tangent lengths

teach.ask: Gappu sees a circle snug inside a four-sided frame: 'Why do the opposite sides add up to the same total?'
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! Equal tangents from each corner make the opposite sides add up the same. Neat!
teach.nudge: What do I know about the two tangents from each corner?

topics.title: Normals, parallel tangents and chapter recap

learn.hook: Every tangent has a partner line at right angles that always heads straight for the centre — meet the normal!
points: The normal at a point P of a circle is the line through P perpendicular to the tangent at P. It always passes through the centre (it lies along the radius).
For any given line l, exactly two tangents of a circle are parallel to l. They touch the circle at the two ends of the diameter perpendicular to l.
The distance between two parallel tangents equals the diameter.
Recap: a tangent meets the circle at one point; the tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact; the two tangents from an external point are equal.

example.q: A circle has centre O and radius 6.5 cm. Two tangents are drawn parallel to a given line l. How far apart are they, and where do they touch the circle?
steps: Draw the diameter AB perpendicular to l
The tangents at A and B are both perpendicular to AB, so both are parallel to l
example.answer: 13 cm apart, touching at the ends of the diameter perpendicular to l

learn.reallife: The two rails a wheel rolls between, or two straight edges gripping a round pipe, are parallel tangents a diameter apart.

games.title: Normals and parallel tangents
items: The normal at a point of a circle passes through the centre.
It is perpendicular to the tangent, so it lies along the radius.
A circle can have exactly one tangent parallel to a given line.
There are always exactly two.
Two parallel tangents are a diameter apart.
They touch at the ends of a diameter.
The tangent and the normal at a point meet at 90°.
That is the definition of the normal.
The tangent at P passes through the centre.
The normal passes through the centre; the tangent is perpendicular to it.

quiz.q: The line through the point of contact, perpendicular to the tangent, always passes through…
quiz.explain: This line is the normal. Since the radius is perpendicular to the tangent, the normal lies along the radius and passes through the centre.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the normal with the radius

quiz.q: Along which line does the normal at a point P of a circle lie?
options: A line parallel to the tangent
quiz.explain: The radius OP is perpendicular to the tangent at P, so the normal at P lies along OP.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the normal with the tangent

quiz.q: How many tangents to a circle can be parallel to a given straight line?
quiz.explain: Exactly two — one at each end of the diameter perpendicular to the given line.
quiz.mistake: Draws one on only one side of the circle

quiz.q: Where do the tangents parallel to a given line l touch the circle?
options: At the ends of the diameter parallel to l
At the ends of the diameter perpendicular to l
quiz.explain: Each tangent is perpendicular to its radius. For it to be parallel to l, that radius must be perpendicular to l, so the points are the ends of the diameter perpendicular to l.
quiz.mistake: Chooses the diameter parallel to l

quiz.q: A circle has radius 6.5 cm. How far apart are the two tangents parallel to a given line?
quiz.explain: The tangents touch at the ends of a diameter, so they are 2 × 6.5 = 13 cm apart.
quiz.mistake: Uses the radius instead of the diameter

quiz.q: Recap: a point P is 17 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 8 cm. How long is the tangent from P?
quiz.explain: The radius is perpendicular to the tangent, so tangent² = 17² − 8² = 289 − 64 = 225, giving 15 cm.
quiz.mistake: Adds the squares instead of subtracting

quiz.q: Recap: PA and PB are tangents from P to a circle with centre O, and ∠AOB = 110°. What is ∠APB?
quiz.explain: In quadrilateral OAPB, ∠A = ∠B = 90°, so ∠AOB + ∠APB = 180°. ∠APB = 180° − 110° = 70°.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the two angles are equal

quiz.q: Recap: at what angle do the tangent and the normal at a point of a circle meet?
quiz.explain: The normal is defined as the line perpendicular to the tangent at the point of contact.
quiz.mistake: Does not remember what 'normal' means

teach.ask: Gappu draws a line l next to a circle and wants two tangents parallel to it. Where should he draw them, and what is the normal?
teach.praise: Tweet! Draw the diameter perpendicular to l and the tangents at its ends — and the normal runs through the centre!
teach.nudge: Which diameter does he need — parallel to l or perpendicular to it?

learn.hook: How far does the tip of a clock's minute hand travel in 20 minutes? Arc length gives the exact answer!
points: Circumference of a circle = 2πr and its area = πr².
An arc is a part of the circle. A minor arc is shorter than a semicircle; a major arc is longer.
An arc that makes angle θ at the centre is θ/360 of the whole circle.
Length of the arc = (θ/360) × 2πr.
Clock facts: the minute hand turns 360° in 60 minutes, so 6° every minute.

example.q: Find the length of an arc that makes 60° at the centre of a circle of radius 21 cm. (π = 22/7)

learn.reallife: Running tracks are curved arcs — race officials use arc lengths to stagger the starting lines fairly.

quiz.q: What is the length of an arc that makes 45° at the centre of a circle of radius 14 cm? (π = 22/7)
quiz.explain: 45° is 1/8 of the circle. Circumference = 2 × 22/7 × 14 = 88 cm, so the arc = 88 ÷ 8 = 11 cm.
quiz.mistake: Uses the area formula πr² instead of 2πr

quiz.q: A clock's minute hand is 21 cm long. How far does its tip travel in 20 minutes? (π = 22/7)
quiz.explain: In 20 minutes the hand turns 120°, which is 1/3 of a circle. 1/3 × 2 × 22/7 × 21 = 44 cm.
quiz.mistake: Uses the whole circumference (132 cm)

quiz.q: An arc of a circle of radius 7 cm is 22 cm long. What angle does it make at the centre? (π = 22/7)
quiz.explain: Circumference = 44 cm. The arc is 22/44 = 1/2 of it, so θ = 180°.
quiz.mistake: Uses the diameter instead of the circumference

quiz.q: The circumference of a circle is 88 cm. What is its radius? (π = 22/7)
quiz.mistake: Finds the diameter (28 cm) instead of the radius

quiz.q: In a circle of radius 7 cm, a minor arc makes 90° at the centre. What is the length of the major arc? (π = 22/7)
quiz.explain: The major arc makes 360° − 90° = 270°. Its length = 270/360 × 44 = 33 cm.
quiz.mistake: Gives the minor arc (11 cm)

quiz.q: A bicycle wheel has radius 35 cm. How far does it roll in 10 complete turns? (π = 22/7)
quiz.explain: One turn = 2 × 22/7 × 35 = 220 cm. Ten turns = 2200 cm = 22 m.
quiz.mistake: Converts centimetres to metres wrongly

quiz.q: Which formula gives the length of an arc making angle θ at the centre?
quiz.explain: An arc is the fraction θ/360 of the whole circumference 2πr.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up arc length with sector area

quiz.q: A pendulum 42 cm long swings through an angle of 60°. How long is the arc its tip travels? (π = 22/7)
quiz.mistake: Divides by 12 instead of 6, or forgets to take the fraction

teach.ask: Gappu watches the clock's minute hand: 'How far does its tip move in 15 minutes?'
teach.praise: Tweet! The angle out of 360, times the circumference. The tip's journey is solved!
teach.nudge: What fraction of the full circle is the arc, and what do I multiply that fraction by?

learn.hook: Cut a round pizza into slices — each slice is a sector, and you can find its exact area!
points: A sector is the region between two radii and the arc joining them.
Area of a sector of angle θ = (θ/360) × πr².
A quadrant (θ = 90°) has area πr²/4, and a semicircle (θ = 180°) has area πr²/2.
Area of the major sector = πr² − area of the minor sector.
Also, area of a sector = ½ × arc length × r.

example.q: Find the area of a sector of angle 60° in a circle of radius 6 cm. (π = 3.14)

learn.reallife: Garden sprinklers that turn through a fixed angle water a sector-shaped patch of lawn.
